why_en: Extend scalar function inputs to ordered components so position and velocity can enter one model while retaining explicit meanings for each input.
Represent each sample as a vector, then stack samples into a matrix to distinguish sample axes from feature axes and verify batch shapes.
Matrix row and column meanings determine compatible inner dimensions and explain how multiple input features combine into multiple outputs.
Each matrix-product entry sums corresponding products; summation indices identify the contracted dimension and distinguish matrix multiplication from elementwise multiplication.
Subtract predicted and target vectors componentwise, then use a norm to convert their errors into a scalar distance for comparing states.
Matrix multiplication applies rotation and translation adds an offset, allowing observations and targets expressed in different frames to be compared consistently.
Orientation has circular geometry; sine and cosine coordinates preserve nearby directions across the angle wraparound boundary when comparing orientations.
Identifying a function's input and output makes its derivative interpretable as local sensitivity, slope, velocity, or another explicitly defined rate of change.
Extend a single-variable derivative by holding other arguments fixed, measuring how one input component changes a multivariable function's output.
Vector component indices identify the particular input or parameter differentiated while all other components remain fixed in a partial derivative.
For a composition, multiply local derivatives along each dependency path to relate the final output change to an earlier variable change.
Multivariable computation graphs contain branching paths; local partial derivatives and summed path contributions extend the chain rule to practical neural networks.
The chain rule computes loss derivatives through multiple model stages; collecting parameter derivatives produces the gradient used for a descent update.
A squared norm turns multidimensional prediction error into a scalar loss, giving parameter gradients a precisely specified optimization objective.
Compute each output's partial derivative with respect to every input, then arrange these derivatives by output rows and input columns.
Jacobian multiplication maps a small input perturbation to an approximate output perturbation; checking dimensions clarifies how actions affect state components.
An eigenvector is mapped to a scalar multiple of itself; interpreting matrix multiplication as a linear transformation explains this preserved direction.
Explicitly define experimental outcomes and events before assigning probabilities, keeping input conditions, events, and their numerical probabilities distinct.
A random variable assigns numerical values to outcomes; probabilities of corresponding events determine its distribution and subsequent uncertainty calculations.
Treat future state as a random variable, then condition on current state and action to express how different actions change future distributions.
Conditional and joint probability identities exchange the roles of evidence and hypothesis, converting observation likelihoods into posterior probabilities of hypotheses.
A random variable specifies possible values and their distribution; expectation weights those values to define average training loss or return.
Discrete expectation multiplies each possible value by its probability and sums over outcomes; the index specifies the complete averaging domain.
Variance averages squared deviations from the mean; covariance averages paired deviations, quantifying dispersion and joint variation between components.
A covariance matrix arranges every pairwise covariance, representing component scales and linear dependence across an entire multivariate distribution.
Gaussian distributions use means for location and variances or covariances for spread; these statistics determine widths and principal elliptical directions.
The exponential term controls how Gaussian density decreases with displacement; taking logarithms exposes the quadratic expression used in optimization.
Sampling standard Gaussian noise and transforming its location and scale generates numerical inputs for diffusion training and candidate-search procedures.
Monte Carlo estimates expectations using finite sample averages; understanding the population quantity clarifies sampling error and the benefit of additional samples.
Write observed data probabilities conditional on inputs or parameters, then hold the observations fixed while comparing alternative parameter explanations.
Differentiate a negative log-likelihood objective with respect to model parameters, updating them to increase the modeled probability of observed data.
Logarithms convert products of small probabilities into sums without changing the maximizing parameters, improving numerical stability and defining an additive loss.
Entropy averages negative log probabilities under the outcome distribution; cross-entropy similarly averages log probabilities assigned by a different model distribution.
Averaging sample negative log likelihoods connects empirical training objectives to cross-entropy, giving probabilistic classification losses an observed-data interpretation.
Negative logarithms penalize low assigned probabilities strongly and make independent information contributions additive, explaining penalties for confidently incorrect predictions.
Subtracting a distribution's entropy from its cross-entropy yields KL divergence, measuring distribution mismatch beyond differences between means alone.
Define a parameterized mapping from inputs to predictions before using labeled examples to adjust its parameters and distinguish training inputs from targets.
Training examples are sampled from a distribution; this motivates adequate task coverage and reserving unseen samples for evaluating learned rules.
Supervised examples supply targets paired with inputs; squared error compares predictions against these targets to construct an explicit scalar training objective.
The squared Euclidean norm sums componentwise prediction errors without sign cancellation and places greater weight on larger numerical deviations.
Average training squared error estimates population expected risk; this distinction separates performance on observed samples from average error on future data.
Summation specifies which samples and state components are accumulated before averaging, allowing implementation reductions and scaling factors to be checked.
Squared error compares linear predictions with target values, converting slope and intercept selection into a measurable and optimizable fitting problem.
Weighted input sums define linear predictions; matrix multiplication applies the same parameters to every sample in a batch efficiently.
Differentiating linear-regression loss with respect to weights and intercept yields an explicit parameter-update loop that introduces neural-network optimization.
Logistic regression retains the weighted linear score, then applies a sigmoid to obtain a binary-class probability between zero and one.
Binary cross-entropy rewards high probability for the observed class and strongly penalizes confident assignments to the incorrect class.
After identifying training examples used for updates, reserve independent validation and test data for hyperparameter selection and final generalization assessment.
Compare fitting error with independent validation error to distinguish insufficient modeling from memorization and diagnose the observed generalization gap.
Squared error provides comparable training and validation metrics and, under suitable regression assumptions, supports bias, variance, and noise decomposition.
Predictions vary across sampled training sets; variance describes this instability separately from systematic error represented by prediction bias.
When predictions are overly sensitive to training data, regularization restricts model complexity; validation monitoring detects excessive constraints that cause underfitting.
Adding a parameter penalty changes loss derivatives and parameter updates, making the effect of regularization strength on weights explicit.
Normalization means and scales are fitted preprocessing parameters; estimate them only from training data and reuse them unchanged for validation and testing.
Standard deviation measures each feature's typical variation; rescaling reduces unit-dependent numerical differences when optimizing or comparing several state components.
Covariance eigenvectors define projection directions and eigenvalues give their variances; retaining largest-eigenvalue directions implements linear principal-component reduction.
PCA selects directions of greatest variance; covariance explains why an oblique projection can preserve more variation than retaining an original coordinate.
PCA depends on feature units and scales; centering and task-appropriate standardization determine how its principal directions should be interpreted.
A weighted mixture of Gaussian components represents multimodal data and extends hard cluster assignments to probabilistic membership in several components.
Independent test data provide evidence about unseen examples; the split unit determines whether evaluation concerns new trajectories, scenes, or other conditions.
Success rates and average errors are finite-sample estimates; sampling variability motivates repeated seeds, additional trials, and uncertainty intervals.
Prediction squared error measures numerical agreement, whereas task success depends on relevant states and closed-loop execution; evaluate both kinds of metrics.
Comparing one-step, multistep, and closed-loop metrics helps identify when predictions leave reliable training coverage under different horizons and task conditions.
Training-validation gaps motivate checking distributional coverage; comparing deployment inputs further distinguishes memorization from encountering previously unobserved state regions.
Exponential and logarithmic functions provide domains, monotonicity, and inverse relationships needed to understand transformations of probabilistic training objectives.
Define the meaning of each repeated term, then use an index to expand compact summation notation into an explicitly checkable calculation.
Vectors introduce an axis containing ordered numerical components; tensors add axes for samples, time, spatial coordinates, and other structured data.
Matrix indexing introduces two-dimensional shapes; tensor notation generalizes these axis and index conventions to higher-order numerical arrays.
Tensor shapes identify the feature axis transformed by a linear layer and which batch or time axes remain unchanged.
Matrix operations combine weighted feature sums into one expression, defining a linear layer's parameter mapping and checking input-output dimensional compatibility.
Each fully connected output is an input-weight dot product; collecting those outputs gives the matrix multiplication used by a linear layer.
An affine layer produces trainable weighted inputs; elementwise nonlinear activation then expands the relationships that a network can represent.
Activation derivatives determine how local input changes propagate and identify saturated regions where gradients become small during training.
Trainable fully connected mappings mix features at successive stages and provide the parameterized transformations composing a multilayer perceptron.
Nonlinear activations between affine layers prevent the entire multilayer network from collapsing algebraically into a single affine transformation.
A loss quantifies the discrepancy between network predictions and targets, specifying the task objective that guides multilayer-perceptron parameter updates.
An MLP supplies a concrete multistage computation graph from input to loss; backpropagation differentiates that graph in reverse dependency order.
The chain rule decomposes loss derivatives into products of local derivatives, providing the mathematical computation performed by each backpropagation path.
The scalar loss initializes reverse differentiation and identifies which prediction discrepancies parameter updates are intended to reduce during training.
Backpropagation computes a minibatch loss gradient; stochastic gradient descent subsequently uses that gradient to update the model parameters.
Expectation relates population training objectives to minibatch averages and explains when sampled gradients estimate the full expected-loss gradient.
Data splits determine which examples may contribute parameter gradients, preventing validation or test information from entering training updates.
SGD introduces gradient-based parameter updates; Adam extends this procedure with accumulated directional statistics and coordinate-dependent update scaling.
First and second moments explain Adam's moving gradient statistics and distinguish the mean squared gradient from gradient variance itself.
Tensor-axis meanings determine which dimensions contribute normalization statistics, distinguishing featurewise operations from statistics taken across a batch.
Means and variances define centering and rescaling, making each statistical operation in a feature-normalization formula explicit and interpretable.
Training-test separation constrains input-standardization statistics, preventing test-data leakage while retaining consistent preprocessing rules during model deployment.
A trainable subnetwork can compute a residual correction; the residual connection adds that correction to the existing input representation.
Backpropagation traces gradients through both the transformed branch and identity path, explaining gradient propagation through deep residual networks.
Spatial and channel axes specify image-tensor organization, allowing convolutional feature-map shapes to be followed through each processing layer.
Fully connected networks introduce trainable weighted sums and nonlinearities; convolution adds local connectivity and parameter sharing across spatial positions.
An MLP supplies a nonlinear state-update function; a recurrent network reuses a shared update function across successive sequence positions.
Tensor shapes separate batch, time, and hidden-feature dimensions, preventing recurrent sequence updates from mixing samples belonging to different trajectories.
An RNN defines dependence on previous hidden states; backpropagation through time expands these recurrent updates into a temporal computation graph.
Ordinary reverse-mode differentiation applies to the unrolled temporal graph, accumulating contributions from parameters reused at multiple time steps.
RNN hidden-state updates establish recurrent sequence modeling; LSTM modifies the update with a cell state and trainable gating mechanisms.
Sigmoid and hyperbolic-tangent activations produce gate coefficients and bounded candidate values, supporting differentiable retention, removal, and addition of memory content.
Exponentiating each score makes it positive; dividing by the sum of exponentials produces normalized nonnegative weights whose total is one.
A score vector represents aligned alternatives; softmax normalizes across those components while preserving each output's correspondence to its input candidate.
Linear projections transform inputs into queries, keys, and values, learning which features determine matching and which information is aggregated.
Softmax converts query-key scores into nonnegative weights summing to one, enabling normalized weighted aggregation of the value vectors.
Matrix multiplication evaluates all query-key dot products together and multiplies the resulting attention-weight matrix by the value matrix.
Attention defines query-key matching and value aggregation; self-attention obtains queries, keys, and values from the same input sequence.
The sequence axis determines attention-matrix row and column meanings, allowing a position-dependent mask to restrict which tokens can be read.
Information-separation principles extend to sequence time: prediction may use only available context, excluding future observations that would reveal the target.
Single-head attention defines one matching-and-aggregation operation; multi-head attention performs several such operations in independently learned projection spaces.
Tensor dimensions specify splitting projected features into attention heads, computing each head, and concatenating outputs along the feature axis.
Self-attention matches content but requires positional information to distinguish sequence order or spatial location when identical content appears at different positions.
Vector addition combines position and content representations of equal width; component organization also explains paired sinusoidal frequencies in positional encodings.
Multi-head attention exchanges information across sequence positions, allowing a Transformer block to combine relations represented in several learned subspaces.
Position encodings provide order or location information that content-only attention cannot independently determine, supporting temporal and spatial interpretation of tokens.
Residual connections add attention and feed-forward updates to existing features, providing direct information and gradient paths through stacked Transformer blocks.
Normalization controls feature scales around sublayers and combines with attention, feed-forward transformations, and residual paths to form a trainable Transformer block.
A Transformer processes token sequences; a Vision Transformer reuses this computation after projecting image patches into token representations.
Image-tensor axes determine conversion from height, width, and channels to patch count and embedding width, enabling shape checks throughout patch projection.
Self-supervision still requires a trainable representation mapping; it changes target construction without requiring a particular visual backbone as a conceptual prerequisite.
A loss converts automatically constructed prediction or cross-view tasks into training signals, replacing the need for manually assigned class labels.
Generalization concepts guide augmentation choices and test whether representations learned without labels transfer to downstream perception or control tasks.
Cross-view consistency alone can permit constant outputs; collapse analysis explains why such low-loss solutions discard distinctions needed for useful representations.
Across-sample expectations and variances measure representation diversity, distinguishing low training loss from retaining meaningful differences among input observations.
Self-supervision constructs targets from related image views; DINO implements this approach using matching between teacher and student output distributions.
Collapse analysis motivates mechanisms beyond view consistency, clarifying the role of centering, temperature, and teacher updates in DINO training.
Softmax with temperature converts teacher and student scores into distributions, enabling cross-view matching through a cross-entropy training objective.
DINO introduces teacher-student self-supervised visual learning; DINOv2 develops its objectives, data organization, and training recipe for stronger general-purpose features.
ViT patch structure explains why DINOv2 can provide global image representations while retaining spatially organized local features for downstream tasks.
Frozen DINOv2 features encode current, future, and goal observations, supplying a common spatial visual representation for DINO-WM prediction and planning.
A Transformer processes action-conditioned feature histories, enabling DINO-WM to predict visual representations after executing candidate action sequences.
Feature-prediction loss supervises the dynamics model using encoded future observations; planning compares predicted terminal features with the encoded goal observation.
Tensor notation makes latent variables dimensionally explicit, distinguishing observation features, initial sampling noise, and internal model states by their origins.
Gaussian distributions provide a common latent prior and sampling source, although latent variables need not be Gaussian or lower-dimensional compressed representations.
A latent representation defines the intermediate encoder output; an autoencoder learns that representation by reconstructing observations from their encoded values.
Trainable MLPs can implement encoder and decoder mappings, providing a basic autoencoder for small fixed-dimensional vector datasets.
Reconstruction loss measures discrepancies between decoded and original inputs and supplies gradients for jointly training the encoder and decoder networks.
A VAE retains encoding and reconstruction while making the encoder probabilistic and regularizing its latent distribution relative to a prior.
Gaussian parameterization supplies means, scales, and a samplable prior; reparameterization constructs differentiable latent samples from these parameters and independent noise.
Backpropagation through reparameterized samples updates encoder distribution parameters and decoder weights, allowing stochastic latent sampling within gradient-based training.
Gaussian noise defines a known corruption process, mixing clean samples and noise at specified levels to construct controlled denoising-training inputs.
Distinguishing latent-variable roles separates noisy intermediate samples from initial noise and prevents diffusion-step indices from being confused with environment time.
A denoising loss specifies the reverse-recovery learning objective, giving the network supervised targets generated by the known forward corruption process.
Diffusion introduces corruption and reverse recovery; DDPM specifies a noise-prediction objective sampled across noise levels and clean training examples.
Backpropagation differentiates discrepancies between predicted and sampled noise through the denoising network, without requiring differentiation through the physical environment.
Minibatch training samples clean examples, Gaussian noise, and noise levels, approximating the multiple expectations in the DDPM training objective.
Conditional generation augments the DDPM denoiser with information such as current state, restricting generated samples to the corresponding conditional future distribution.
Conditional distributions permit several futures from one state; expected-value reasoning explains why averaging those futures can produce an infeasible intermediate state.
Conditional generation fixes the current-state context; deterministic DDIM then maps initial noise to a sample under that specified condition.
A DDPM-trained denoiser can support DDIM sampling; distinguish the network's training objective from the reverse sampling procedure selected at inference.
Deterministic DDIM maps fixed initial noise to repeatable subgoals, allowing ID-WM to compare candidates and optimize noise as a high-level decision.
The latent-variable distinction identifies searched noise as a generator input, rather than an actuator command or an observed visual feature.
Optimizer updates specify how training modifies network weights, contrasting with deployment-time planning that optimizes action or noise decisions under fixed weights.
DDIM inference can repeatedly call the denoiser; frozen weights do not imply a single forward pass or low inference computation.
Transformer forward computation describes one prediction, while planning evaluates many candidates repeatedly; model-call latency therefore differs from complete decision latency.
Ordered vectors combine position, orientation, velocity, and other quantities into defined inputs, executable actions, and supervised state-prediction targets.
Rotation uses matrix multiplication and translation uses vector addition; matrix shapes and composition order determine the direction of coordinate conversion.
Positions and directions first require vector representations tied to explicit reference frames before coordinate transformations have unambiguous inputs and outputs.
Define predicted state variables and available controls before specifying dynamics, ensuring relevant velocity, contact, and other required information is included.
Velocity differentiates position with respect to time, and acceleration differentiates velocity, connecting static configurations to time-dependent state transitions.
A single observation may omit velocity or contact information; earlier observations and actions can supplement prediction through a history window.
Conditional probability specifies which history is available when predicting the next state and clarifies whether current observation alone is sufficient.
Dynamics predict action consequences; feedback compares predictions with new measurements and revises subsequent control to address execution discrepancies.
A norm converts the vector difference between predicted terminal state and goal into a scalar score for ranking candidate action sequences.
Specify whether the goal includes block position, orientation, or pusher position before defining the appropriate errors and task-success criteria.
Repeated application of a one-step transition model produces a rollout, making earlier prediction errors part of later model inputs.
One-step supervised error evaluates a single transition; multistep evaluation measures error growth with horizon, so these metrics cannot be substituted indiscriminately.
Search ranks candidate sequences using goal costs and restricts acceptable solutions using action, collision, and time constraints relevant to the task.
Continuous action spaces cannot be exhaustively enumerated; random sampling provides a finite-budget procedure for exploring possible decision sequences.
Random shooting approximates a high-dimensional decision search by sampling a finite set of action sequences and evaluating each candidate's cost.
Each sampled action sequence requires repeated forward prediction before its terminal state can be scored and compared against other candidates.
CEM retains sampling, rollout, and scoring, adding elite selection and proposal refitting so later candidate samples exploit information from previous iterations.
A Gaussian proposal with adjustable means and variances generates candidates; elite sample statistics update the proposal parameters for subsequent iterations.
Averaging elite candidates estimates a new mean, and averaging their centered squared deviations estimates variance for Gaussian proposal refitting.
CEM solves one finite-horizon optimization problem; MPC invokes such optimization repeatedly after executing actions and observing the resulting state.
Feedback supplies newly observed execution states as planning initial conditions; MPC specifies the repeated planning, partial execution, and observation schedule.
Identical geometric positions can have different short-horizon reachable sets under different velocities or input limits, so reachability must include dynamics and time.
A goal specifies a desired endpoint; reachability additionally requires an admissible path satisfying dynamics, obstacle restrictions, and action constraints.
Policies map states or observations to actions; value functions must likewise specify the state or state-action condition whose outcomes they evaluate.
Transition and policy randomness produce different future reward sequences; value functions average discounted returns across these possible trajectories.
Episode-level offline splits reveal differences between training coverage and planned states while preventing adjacent-frame leakage from obscuring generalization failures.
Distinguishing training error from generalization error explains why accurate fitting on offline transitions can still fail in states selected by planning.
Rollouts propagate prediction error, while planning selects apparently favorable trajectories; together these mechanisms can magnify failures outside training coverage.
The high-level generator supplies local future-state alternatives; integrating it into ID-WM requires tracking its conditioning inputs, generated subgoals, and interface to local control.
The low-level model predicts action consequences while search selects actions; the overview integrates these distinct computations with high-level subgoal generation.
Temporal hierarchy composes local transitions into longer plans; the overview connects subgoal-chain organization with the models that generate and realize each transition.
The high-level objective balances goal progress and noise regularization; integrating it specifies how candidate subgoal chains are scored within the complete method.
The training-inference dataflow distinguishes learned model weights from searched decisions and connects both levels to actual execution and subsequent observation.
Condition on current state and train against a later state to model the multimodal distribution of local futures at the selected temporal offset.
After training, deterministic DDIM converts initial noise into candidate future states, allowing the high-level planner to call the generator repeatedly.
Local temporal targets approximate reachable future structure from data; low-level realization and evaluation remain necessary checks on generated subgoal feasibility.
With fixed model and current-state condition, deterministic DDIM maps each initial noise vector to a future state, enabling subgoal selection through noise search.
A standard Gaussian defines the noise prior without assigning physical meanings to individual coordinates; extreme searched values may cause out-of-distribution generation.
Search over continuous generator inputs replaces high-level direct optimization of a long primitive-action sequence, delegating candidate-state construction to the learned mapping.
The low-level Transformer combines state-action history with action embeddings to predict the next state, supplying context-dependent local dynamics evaluations.
Repeated low-level forward prediction evaluates each candidate action sequence and estimates its terminal distance from the requested subgoal.
CEM proposes and refines action sequences; forward-model outcome evaluation turns this search into an inverse solution from desired subgoal to executable actions.
Allowing planning to optimize noise can move generator inputs beyond common prior regions, motivating a penalty on extreme noise-coordinate magnitudes.
Terminal distance defines high-level goal error as a scalar objective; an additional noise penalty controls undesirable generator inputs during optimization.
A weighted regularizer combines goal progress with avoidance of extreme noise in one candidate score, explicitly trading off these planning preferences.
Each high-level transition must match the low-level time budget; geometric proximity alone does not establish that local control can realize the subgoal.
Long action sequences increase search dimension; hierarchical subgoal chains separate long-horizon route organization from local executable-action optimization.
Generate a local future from one state, then condition the next generation on that result to compose a sequence of subgoals.
High-level training uses temporally separated state pairs, whereas inference generates candidate subgoals; tracking both flows separates supervised targets from online inputs.
Low-level training uses action-conditioned next-state targets, while inference rolls out candidates to choose actions; these different uses must be recorded explicitly.
High-level candidate scoring combines terminal goal distance and noise regularization so CEM elite selection ranks candidates according to the complete objective.
Place high- and low-level searches inside an observe-execute-observe cycle to define online planning, state updates, and task termination conditions.
ID-WM retains action-conditioned feature prediction and low-level planning from DINO-WM, adding a local future-state generator for organizing longer tasks.
Understanding denoising objectives enables comparison between diffusion that generates complete trajectories and diffusion that generates local future states for subsequent search.
Policy and value concepts clarify how hierarchical reinforcement-learning baselines differ from model-based goal search and identify their additional training dependencies.
Fixed training, validation, and test boundaries determine whether new-goal performance reflects generalization rather than leaked evaluation information.
Offline coverage and planning-induced distribution differences affect success, motivating evaluation of distribution shifts, failures, and data-augmentation settings.
Execution, replanning, and search budgets determine fair measurements of success rate, completion steps, and end-to-end decision latency.
Implement mathematical vectors as arrays while preserving feature meanings and order, then apply indexing, broadcasting, and batched numerical operations.
Array and function operations become tensors and modules, requiring explicit management of shapes, numerical types, and device placement.
Automatic differentiation implements the chain rule; backward computes gradients, and the optimizer subsequently uses those gradients to update model parameters.
Array slicing constructs aligned histories, actions, and future labels, then organizes them into batches with explicitly checkable numerical shapes.
Split episodes before constructing windows, preventing neighboring frames or future portions of the same trajectory from crossing evaluation boundaries.
History windows must retain predictive information while avoiding reset boundaries and excluding future target observations from the model input.
A runnable training loop is an initial check; reproduction additionally requires saved configurations, prediction-error measurements, closed-loop evaluation, and timing.
Fix dataset versions and window-index manifests so different experimental runs use the same training inputs and evaluation examples.
Derive reproduction acceptance checks from the paper's metrics and ablations, rather than relying solely on one successful demonstration video.
Record configurations, prediction errors, task outcomes, and failure trajectories at each implementation stage so claimed progress remains independently inspectable.
Decompose ID-WM into separately verifiable stages covering data preparation, dynamics, sampling-based planning, hierarchical integration, and visual-representation extensions.
LSTM modifies recurrent state updates using gates and a memory cell, addressing long-term gradient propagation within the broader recurrent-network family.
CNNs exploit local spatial structure, whereas RNNs exploit recurrent temporal structure; these branches can be learned independently according to task requirements.
Both support sequence modeling, but Transformers use attention rather than recurrent updates; LSTM is not a mandatory mathematical prerequisite for Transformer formulas.
DINOv2 develops scalable self-supervised visual-feature training from the DINO approach; representation quality still requires evaluation on relevant downstream tasks.
ID-WM retains low-level prediction and planning from state or visual-feature histories and actions, then adds high-level organization of future subgoals.
DDIM provides sampling updates compatible with denoising training; deterministic settings make initial noise a repeatable, searchable high-level decision variable.
Retain finite-horizon optimization and feedback execution, then add subgoals to separate long-horizon route organization from detailed local action selection.
Robot dynamics provide application context; the paper evaluates Wall, PushT, and Maze, so G1 transfer requires additional state, contact, and control validation.
Both concern representations, but PCA uses linear maximum-variance projection and learned latent spaces may be nonlinear; PCA is not required for DINO training.
PCA can preprocess representations before clustering, but neither K-means nor Gaussian-mixture modeling inherently requires applying PCA before fitting clusters.
These nodes explain the same noise-to-decision connection from generative modeling and planning perspectives, allowing the role of initial noise to be compared.
